analysis.one_liner: Bars nursing homes from evicting residents because they rely on Medicaid to pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee; it was introduced in May 1998 and died without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend Medicaid law to stop nursing homes from transferring or discharging a resident simply because the resident's care is paid through Medicaid instead of out of the resident's own pocket. If a nursing home stops taking Medicaid patients altogether, it would still have to keep Medicaid-covered residents already living there and keep receiving Medicaid payments for them. The only carve-out is that a home could still refuse to accept a Medicaid patient as a new admission.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents who run out of private money and turn to Medicaid, plus their families. Today a home can discharge a resident once Medicaid becomes the payer, since Medicaid typically pays less than private pay; this bill would lock in protection for residents once admitted. The bill also protects residents when a facility exits the Medicaid program entirely.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a nursing facility from transferring or discharging any resident on the basis of the resident's eligibility for Medicaid payment for facility services.

If a facility stops being a Medicaid-participating provider, it is still treated as one for residents already there who qualify for Medicaid, so payments continue and compliance requirements stay in force — the home cannot use its exit from Medicaid as a way to empty out Medicaid beds.
Clarifies that a facility's withdrawal from Medicaid cannot be construed as a 'failure to pay' by an eligible resident, closing the loophole homes could otherwise use to discharge for nonpayment.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing homes. Medicaid generally reimburses less than private-pay rates, so homes that currently discharge residents when their private funds run out would have to keep and continue caring for them at the Medicaid rate. Homes leaving the Medicaid program would have to keep honoring it for residents already there.

drawbacks.text: The requirement applies only to residents already admitted; a facility can still refuse any individual as a new resident, so the bill protects people already inside the door but not those seeking admission.

Nursing homes would absorb the gap between Medicaid payment rates and private-pay rates for protected residents, a cost that could pressure margins at facilities that already say Medicaid rates underfund care.
The obligation applies indefinitely for a facility that exits Medicaid, which keeps the home providing services at a rate it no longer contractually agreed to for those residents.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection is modest and well-targeted: it stops a real, documented practice of evicting residents whose money has run out, and it lets facilities decline new Medicaid admissions so the burden is limited. The cost falls on facilities in the form of lower-margin Medicaid stays. It was a narrow fix rather than a broad overhaul of Medicaid payment rates, which is arguably the root problem, but on its own terms it traded a small, definable cost to operators for strong protection of a vulnerable population.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Graham introduced the bill on May 11, 1998, joined by original cosponsors including Republicans John Chafee and Charles Grassley and Democrats Tom Harkin and Tim Johnson.
The bill's only action after introduction was being read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
The Finance Committee held no markup and the Senate took no further action before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators are better off, since they can still discharge residents once Medicaid becomes the payer. No one else gained from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Bob Graham
for.role: U.S. Senator from Florida; bill sponsor

for.name: Sens. Chafee, Johnson, Harkin, and Grassley
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan support from the start.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, for a total of 8 senators supporting it.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 11, 1998 and never reported it out; no hearing or markup appears in the record.

against.name: Sen. William Roth
against.what_they_did: As chairman, controlled the committee calendar and never scheduled action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — 2 of the 7 cosponsors were Republicans (Chafee and Grassley) and 5 were Democrats — so the bill's death cannot be traced to a partisan vote; no vote ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill would end the practice of discharging residents once their private funds run out and Medicaid pays the bill at a lower rate, and would keep facilities bound to Medicaid for residents already in the building even if they exit the program. Operators' financial interest in preferring private-pay residents runs directly against the residents' need for a place to live.
Residents who spend down to Medicaid would keep their beds and their care instead of facing eviction at the moment they become poorest.
